objectives.text: Name the three classes of lipid and say which makes up most body and food fat.
Distinguish saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids.
Describe how fat is digested and why bile is needed.
Distinguish LDL from HDL and say why the labels 'bad' and 'good' are used.
Explain what hydrogenation produces and why it matters for health.
Name the main causes of foodborne illness and the practices that prevent it.

terms.gloss: Three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone. Most body fat and most food fat.
Carbon chain filled with hydrogen, no double bonds. Usually solid at room temperature.
Made by the liver, stored in the gallbladder. Emulsifies fat so enzymes can reach it.
The lipoprotein that carries absorbed long-chain fat out through the lymph.
Low protein, high cholesterol. High levels are associated with cardiovascular risk.
Adding hydrogen to unsaturated fat to harden it. Produces trans fat as a by-product.

questions.prompt: Which lipid class makes up most of both body fat and food fat?
questions.why: Three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone — the storage form, and what 'fats and oils' means on a label.
distractorNotes: Structural, chiefly in cell membranes.
Cholesterol belongs here; a small fraction of the total.
Not one of the three classes.

questions.prompt: A fatty acid that is solid at room temperature is most likely:
questions.why: Saturated chains pack together tightly. Double bonds kink the chain and keep it liquid.
distractorNotes: Several double bonds; liquid at room temperature.
One double bond; usually liquid.
Being trans-free says nothing about the state.

questions.prompt: What does bile actually do to fat?
questions.why: Bile is a detergent, not an enzyme. It breaks fat into droplets so lipase has surface to work on.
distractorNotes: That is lipase's job.
Absorption happens at the lining, not by bile.
Fat is not converted to glucose.

questions.prompt: Absorbed long-chain fat leaves the intestine by which route?
options: The portal vein, as free fat
The bile duct, back to the liver
questions.why: Chylomicrons are too large for the capillaries, so they enter the lymph first and join the blood later.
distractorNotes: That is the route for sugars and amino acids.
Bile flows toward the gut, not away.
Fat is absorbed well before the colon.

questions.prompt: Why is LDL called the 'bad' cholesterol?
options: High levels track with heart risk
It is chemically a different sterol
It is the only one carrying fat
It cannot be measured in blood
questions.why: LDL is low in protein and high in cholesterol, and high levels are associated with cardiovascular disease. HDL runs the other way.
distractorNotes: The cholesterol is identical; the carrier differs.
Several lipoproteins carry lipid.
It is routinely measured.

questions.prompt: Hydrogenation is used by manufacturers mainly because it:
options: Extends shelf life and firms texture
Lowers the calories in the fat
Strips the cholesterol out of the oil
questions.why: Hardened oils resist oxidation and keep longer. The cost is trans fat formed at the same time.
distractorNotes: The energy content is unchanged.
Vegetable oils have no cholesterol to remove.
It runs the other way — it saturates.

questions.prompt: Recommended fat intake for adults is what share of total calories?
questions.why: Within that band, saturated fat is kept under 10 percent of calories, and trans fat as low as possible.
distractorNotes: Too low; essential fatty acids would be at risk.
That is closer to the carbohydrate range.
Far too low to be workable or healthy.

questions.prompt: What most raises unfavourable blood cholesterol for most people?
questions.why: Cholesterol in food affects blood cholesterol less than many assume; the fats eaten alongside it matter more.
distractorNotes: Its effect is smaller than commonly believed.
Protein is not the main driver.
Fibre tends to help, not harm.

questions.prompt: The single most effective everyday guard against foodborne illness is:
options: Washing hands and separating raw foods
Rinsing raw meat under the tap
Keeping cooked food at room temperature
Relying on smell to judge safety
questions.why: Hand hygiene and preventing cross-contamination do more than any single other habit. Temperature control is the other half.
distractorNotes: Rinsing raw meat spreads bacteria around the sink.
The danger zone is exactly where bacteria multiply.
Many pathogens leave no smell at all.

questions.prompt: Leaving cooked food in the danger zone is risky because:
options: Bacteria multiply fastest at those temperatures
Nutrients break down and are lost
Fat separates out of the dish
Food takes up airborne bacteria from the kitchen
questions.why: Between refrigeration and hot-holding temperatures, bacterial growth is rapid. Time at that range is what accumulates risk.
distractorNotes: Some loss occurs, but it is not the safety issue.
Not a food-safety mechanism.
Airborne contamination is not the main route.

checklist: Pick one fat-containing food and name which lipid class dominates it.
Say whether its fatty acids are mainly saturated, mono- or polyunsaturated.
Follow it through emulsification, digestion and absorption.
Say one swap that would improve its saturated-fat profile.
selfCheck: Did I say why bile is needed before lipase can work?
Did I name the route absorbed fat takes out of the gut?
applicationPrompts.aiPolicy: These are questions for you to answer. This app does not write any part of a submission.
